card.tagline: A traditional Greek folk dance echoing the rhythm of hauling fishing nets.
card.profile: The Trata is a traditional Greek commemorative folk dance performed in Megara in Attica as well as across the Aegean Islands. Executed on the Tuesday following Easter in alternate years, women in Megara gather in the open space before the chapel of Saint John the Dancer to dance the Trata. While local tradition connects the custom to the construction of the chapel in a single day during Ottoman rule, folklorists note its net-hauling movements point to an ancient origin designed to secure a good catch. In the Aegean Islands, it takes the form of a Syrtos danced to a specific traditional song.
card.insight: Danced every two years on Bright Tuesday in Megara, the Trata features movements mimicking the hauling in of fishing nets, linking modern local tradition to ancient maritime rites.

card.profile_long:
The Trata represents a distinctive thread in Greek folk choreography, bridging mainland Attica with the Aegean Islands through rhythmic movement and maritime tradition. In the town of Megara, located in Attica, the dance is held as a biennial commemorative event. Every alternate year, on the Tuesday immediately following Easter Sunday, the women of Megara gather in the open plaza facing the tiny chapel dedicated to Saint John the Dancer. According to popular belief in Megara, the dance commemorates the legendary building of this chapel during the era of Ottoman Greece, an effort said to have been accomplished within the span of a single day. The performance before Saint John the Dancer serves as a living connection between local history, community identity, and religious commemoration.

Beyond popular local legend, folklorists point toward a deeper, pre-Ottoman origin for the dance. The physical movements of the Trata explicitly mimic the rhythmic pulling and hauling in of heavy fishing nets from the sea. Folkloric research suggests that the dance is far older than the Ottoman period, likely originating in antiquity as a ritualized action executed to ensure prosperous fishing trips and bountiful catches for local fishermen. The symbolic representation of fishing remains central to the dance's identity, capturing the physical tension and cooperative labor of coastal life within a structured celebratory movement.

While Megara presents a specific biennial ritual context, the Trata manifests across the Aegean Islands in everyday social life. In the islands, the term refers to a variant of the Syrtos dance set specifically to the song Η τράτα μας η κουρελού. Unlike the strictly timed biennial event in Megara, the island variant is performed at all types of social functions, celebrations, and community gatherings. Regional nuances exist across the archipelagos; for instance, on the North East Aegean island of Ikaria, dancers execute the Trata with distinct specific movements during the musical chorus. Across both mainland and island contexts, the dance maintains its core thematic bond to maritime labor and communal celebration.

Technically, the dance relies on continuous spatial group cohesion, moving in line or circle formations suited to open spaces and public gatherings. In Megara, the participation of women in front of Saint John the Dancer forms a solemn yet celebratory spectacle, while island performances encourage general social participation. Music for the Aegean variant is rooted in Nisiotika island folk traditions, maintaining a steady rhythmic foundation suitable for the Syrtos step structure. Through its dual role as a sacred site commemorative dance in Megara and a versatile social dance across the Aegean, the Trata continues to preserve ancient maritime motifs within contemporary Greek cultural practice.
